newsitem.title: INDONESIA: S.E. Asian Cocoa - Prices mixed, watch weather.
newsitem.headline: S.E. Asian Cocoa - Prices mixed, watch weather.

text.p: Southeast Asian cocoa prices were mixed on Wednesday, with Malaysian values stable while levels in Indonesia dipped following a sharp fall in New York overnight as players monitored weather developments, traders said.
They said there had been no noticeable impact of the El Nino weather pattern on output, but added that there was concern over the mid-crop harvest in Indonesia expected later this year.
"Supply seems to be tight, but this could be due to sellers waiting for the right price," one Indonesian trader said.

"There has also been uneven pod development in some parts of Sulawesi because of problems with weather last year," he said. "I think the next batch of pods will mature in August. Players are watching weather developments closely."
Other traders said demand had been good following gains in New York earlier in the week. "Many contracts are being signed by exporters, who seem to be filling orders," one said.
The trader said arrivals in Ujung Pandang, capital of the key growing region of South Sulawesi, have been steady but added that the main crop harvest underway now could have no peak.
"The flow has been rather even, instead of like previous years when we saw sudden jumps in production," he added.
The trader said the feeling in the industry was that the mid-crop harvest could take place sooner than usual in October because of the change in the production pattern.
"We might just see the harvest period extending without a pause," he said. "This would mean that we will be running out of beans sooner this year."

The traders said fair, average quality cocoa was quoted at 3,300-3,350 rupiah/kg at Ujung Pandang, compared with 3,550-3,600 a week ago. The price in the North Sumatran city of Medan was quoted 3,675 rupiah/kg, against 3,450 rupiah.
In New York, the September contract closed $28 down at $1,685 a tonne on Tuesday, while spot July fell $26 to $1,658.
In Malaysia, prices of beans were virtually unchanged from levels on Tuesday and last week, with sellers retaining their price quotes on expectations of sufficient demand.
Most grinders have indicated that they had an adequate supply of beans, despite a weak main harvest in the first half of the year, trade sources said.
"Their concept of enough can be interpreted in two ways," said Khoo Hon Syn, chairman of the Sabah Cocoa Dealers Association in Malaysia.
"They could mean that they have enough beans to grind or don't want to take any more because they can't sell cocoa butter at decent prices due to depressed ratios," Khoo said.
He said although sellers, or farmers, were confident of the grinding patterns of their clients "the other question we should also look at is whether consumption is going to match this".
Traders said the Malaysian market was currently mixed with local and Indonesian beans, as well as those from Papua New Guinea, Ghana and the Solomon Islands.

On Wednesday, the Malaysian Cocoa Board quoted the SMC 1A out of Tawau, the country's main growing area on the eastern Sabah state, at an average of 4,000 ringgit a tonne. Grade 1B, also out of Tawau, was quoted at an average of 3,950 ringgit.

Both prices were unchanged from last week. But if compared to Tuesday, the IA was down 20 ringgit while the IB was lower by 10 ringgit. On Wednesday, traders quoted the 1A at an average of 4,050 and the 1B at 3,970-3,980.
